Partial-recovery interval for the Event Clock

Source: R/spanning.R
ec_recovery_set.Rd

A traded event price can move for two reasons: news about the outcome, or a change in how the market values the two outcomes relative to each other. Under exact recovery only the first moves log odds continuously, and the measured log-odds variation is the physical Event Clock. Partial recovery allows the valuation gap to contribute too, but at most a fraction \(\delta^2\) of the measured variation, \([\upsilon]^c \le \delta^2 [L]^c\). The physical clock then lies in the sharp interval $$(1-\delta)_+^2\,\widehat{A} \;\le\; A \;\le\; (1+\delta)^2\,\widehat{A},$$ where \(\widehat{A}\) is the measured log-odds variation. Exact recovery is \(\delta = 0\). The lower end is the "low-clock endpoint" used for conservative sensitivity analysis: at \(\delta = 0.5\) it scales the measured clock by \((1 - 0.5)^2 = 0.25\).

Usage

ec_recovery_set(A, delta = c(0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5), eps = NULL)

Arguments

A

Measured log-odds quadratic variation (e.g. the A column of event_clock(), or a forecast from event_clock_forecast()).

delta

Partial-recovery bound(s) \(\delta \ge 0\); the default is a sensitivity grid up to the deliberately wide \(\delta = 0.5\).

eps

Deprecated alias for delta (the argument name used up to version 0.4.0).

Value

A tibble with columns A, delta, lower, upper (one row per A \(\times\) delta combination).

References

Hanke, Schadner, Stöckl, and Weissensteiner (Working Paper), "The Event Clock: What State Prices Identify About Physical Information".

Examples

ec_recovery_set(0.511)                   # Brexit 1M clock
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>       A delta lower upper
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 0.511  0    0.511 0.511
#> 2 0.511  0.1  0.414 0.618
#> 3 0.511  0.25 0.287 0.798
#> 4 0.511  0.5  0.128 1.15 
ec_recovery_set(c(0.064, 0.166), delta = 0.5)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>       A delta  lower upper
#>   <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 0.064   0.5 0.016  0.144
#> 2 0.166   0.5 0.0415 0.374
